transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-08
Time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Solutions), Priya Desai (Orion Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (Orion SRE), Noah Kim (Orion PM)

[00:00] Alex Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. Quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, AE for Redwood. Samira will run through Optimize recommendations focused on batching and caching and then we can jump into your specific questions.
[00:20] Priya Desai: Thanks Alex. From Orion side, Priya here, Liam and Noah are on the call. We're primarily evaluating ways to lower token cost for our fraud detection and reconciliation prompts without blowing up tail latency.
[00:28] Samira Khan: Great, that's exactly what this walkthrough is about. I'll start with the high level

batching, prefix (aka KV) cache, and then show a simple cost model. There'll be some slides, and then we can map it to your traffic.
[01:05] Samira Khan: So first, batching. Redwood supports continuous batching with configurable windows. You can tune "max wait" and "max batch size". For low-latency endpoints we recommend small max_wait (10-30ms) and smaller batch sizes; for high throughput background jobs, larger batch and a higher window to maximize GPU utilization.
[01:40] Liam O'Connor: Quick q — in production our spikes at EOD are huge, will large batch windows cause queueing and latency spikes for interactive flows?
[01:50] Samira Khan: Good call. That's where routing policies and request classification come in. You can tag interactive traffic and route to low-latency pool with stricter batching. Also you can set overflow policies to fall back to a cheaper model or dedicated hot lane.
[02:15] Noah Kim: Does the runtime do automatic batching per-model or per-route?
[02:20] Samira Khan: Per-route. So you create a route for fraud-touchpoints with specific batching config. The runtime groups by route/model and then schedules on GPU.
[02:45] Samira Khan: Moving to caching. Two patterns we talk about: prefix caching (response prefix caching / prompt caching) and KV cache (key-value cache for long-lived contexts). Prefix cache is great when you have repeatable prompts or system messages that are costly; KV cache is ideal for multi-turn chat or when you need long context and can cache KV states between tokens.
[03:20] Priya Desai: For our reconciliation flow, we often hit the same system instructions and company templates — sounds like prefix cache would help a lot?
[03:30] Samira Khan: Exactly. If you have high reuse of system templates or boilerplate, prefix caching can hit 40-70% of tokens depending on reuse. Realistically we'd need examples to estimate.
[03:50] Alex Park: We'll show a quick cost model — high level example: assume 1M requests/day, avg 200 tokens/request, 30% prefix cache hit, and batching saves 20% GPU cost under typical distribution — that'll reduce total cost significantly.
[04:25] Liam O'Connor: How do you calculate the batching savings? Is it purely GPU utilization or are there other factors?
[04:35] Samira Khan: It's mostly GPU utilization and reduced per-token overhead. Smaller model context size and KV cache hit rates also change compute. In the cost model we break down: tokens served, tokens generated on GPU, cache hits (prefix/KV) which avoid re-executing prefix, and then GPU-second cost which maps to $/hour of instance and amortized across tokens.
[05:05] Noah Kim: Any micros on latency impact? We have a 95th latency SLO at 300ms for interactive APIs.
[05:15] Samira Khan: For interactive flows with strict SLO you typically use small batching windows (10-30ms), pin to low-latency instances, and avoid KV cache misses that require recomputation. KV cache speeds up multi-turn by not recomputing previous tokens but a cold miss costs you. We recommend a hybrid: prefix cache for shared system content plus KV cache for per-session context.
[05:45] Priya Desai: What's the integration effort? We run in AWS with some on-prem sensitive data. Can we use Redwood Hosted for most traffic and private for regulated flows?
[05:55] Alex Park: Yes, hybrid routing is common. Hosted API for non-sensitive, and Redwood Dedicated or Private for regulated flows. You can use same API and routing policies. For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption at rest.
[06:20] Liam O'Connor: On encryption — do you store KV cache contents? We have concerns about PII in cache states.
[06:30] Samira Khan: Good question. KV cache can be configured not to persist to disk, to be TTL'd, or to be encrypted with customer-managed keys. We support KMS integrations and audit logs for cache access. We'll share the security docs.
[06:55] Alex Park: I'll drop the SOC2/infra doc link after this call.
[07:05] Samira Khan: Back to cost model — here's a simplified spreadsheet I use. Example assumptions: 1M req/day, 200 tokens/req, prefix hit 30% (those tokens avoid re-execution), KV hit 20% for multi-turn sessions, baseline GPU cost $X/hr. With those numbers batching improved utilization by ~20% in our simulations which yields approx 18-22% cost savings.
[07:45] Priya Desai: Is that 20% batching improvement realistic for payments workloads? Our prompts vary a lot.
[07:55] Samira Khan: It depends on request size distribution. Payments often have many small requests which batch well on the same model. For highly heterogeneous token sizes you may see less. That's why we asked for your traffic profile as a next step.
[08:20] [Slide share noise: Samira presenting spreadsheet]
[08:45] Samira Khan: Here's a per-token breakdown: tokens served, tokens generated, cache hits, GPU-seconds. Cache hit assumptions directly reduce tokens executed on GPU. Note also that prefix cache can reduce both tokens sent to model and tokens generated, while KV cache mainly reduces recomputation for multi-turn.
[09:10] Liam O'Connor: Do you have metrics on cold start impact for KV cache?
[09:15] Samira Khan: Cold misses cost the full compute for that session, but we typically have warm pools or pre-warming strategies for high concurrency sessions. Also you can set a persistent cache for long-running sessions in Dedicated.
[09:35] Noah Kim: For our reconciliation chatbots, sessions are short (2-3 turns) so KV might not help much. Prefix seems more applicable.
[09:45] Samira Khan: Makes sense — prefix cache generally gives bigger wins for few-turn flows with repeated system content.
[10:05] Alex Park: Let's talk numbers — I want to show a concrete example with 30% prefix hit and 20% batching uplift versus a no-cache baseline.
[10:15] Samira Khan: Baseline: 1M reqs * 200 tokens = 200M tokens/day. GPU executes 200M tokens. If prefix hit 30% (60M tokens avoided) and batching reduces GPU time by 20% on the remaining 140M tokens, effectively GPU token-equivalent drops to ~112M tokens — big delta. Then map GPU-seconds -> $/day.
[10:50] Priya Desai: Do you have a calculator we can run with our numbers?
[10:55] Samira Khan: Yes, I'll send the spreadsheet and we can populate with your distribution. The spreadsheet also includes sensitivity for prefix hit rates (10-70%) and batching windows.
[11:10] [Transcription note: slight audio cut for ~3s]
[11:20] Liam O'Connor: Can the prefix cache be invalidated easily? We roll system messages fairly often.
[11:25] Samira Khan: Yes, prefix cache entries can be invalidated via API or TTLs, and you can tag entries for automated refresh. Typical pattern is TTL of 24-72 hours for templates that change frequently.
[11:40] Noah Kim: How does caching interact with model rollouts? We do A/B model tests and need consistency.
[11:50] Samira Khan: Redwood ties cache entries to model version. When you roll models we can either invalidate cache or maintain versioned caches so you don't get stale behavior across variants. We support canary rollouts with cache scoping to variant.
[12:10] Priya Desai: On the deployment side, what are the latency differences between Hosted and Dedicated?
[12:20] Jordan Li: Hosted can be very low-latency in our public regions but Dedicated gives you predictability and isolation; tail latency SLA is better on Dedicated because you control instance sizing and hot lanes. Hosted is simplest for dev/prod non-sensitive traffic.
[12:40] Priya Desai: We're leaning towards hybrid. Some regulated reconciliation flows must stay in our VPC.
[12:45] Alex Park: Totally supported — Private deployment in VPC or on-prem with same API surface. We'll share network diagram and supported connectivity.
[12:55] Liam O'Connor: Any third-party dependencies? We want to avoid vendor lock for cache storage.
[13:05] Samira Khan: KV cache is managed by Redwood runtime but can be configured to persist into your object store or in-memory only. For Private you can point it to your stores. We'll share config examples.
[13:30] Priya Desai: Let's dig deeper into prefix cache eviction strategy — in high churn days will cache thrash?
[13:40] Samira Khan: We have LRU eviction and size TTLs. For templated content it's stable; for highly dynamic content we recommend shorter TTLs or relying more on batching and fallback models. Also, you can tag cache keys by tenant to avoid cross-tenant eviction interference.
[14:05] Noah Kim: Curious about our expected cost savings range — ballpark?
[14:10] Samira Khan: For payments we've seen 15-35% cost reduction with prefix caching + batching depending on reuse and request mixing. 15% is conservative, 35% is for highly templated workloads.
[14:30] Priya Desai: What about impact on output quality? Any chance caching causes stale prompts or hallucinations?
[14:40] Samira Khan: Cache doesn't change model outputs except for removing repeated token generation; but stale system prompts can change behavior which is why TTLs and invalidation are important. Redwood's rollout tooling helps test cached vs uncached variants.
[14:55] [00:15 pause, background typing]
[15:10] Alex Park: Let's map this to your timeline. Priya, you mentioned a pilot in Q4?
[15:20] Priya Desai: Yes, we'd like a pilot: evaluate cost savings and run 1 week of production-like traffic. Security sign-off is the gating factor.
[15:28] Alex Park: Ok action items: Samira will send the spreadsheet and config snippets; Priya will send traffic profile; we'll plan a Dedicated benchmark once we have that.
[15:40] Liam O'Connor: For the benchmark, can Redwood run it in our VPC or do we need to send traffic to hosted?
[15:48] Jordan Li: We can run Dedicated inside your VPC or set up a private pilot. For an initial run we often do a controlled test in hosted with synthetic traffic, then move to a VPC/Dedicated run once security approves.
[16:05] Noah Kim: Pricing — how does Dedicated pricing compare? We need rough numbers to build economic case.
[16:12] Alex Park: I'll follow up with a detailed pricing sheet but high level: Dedicated is commit-based (monthly/annual) — predictable unit cost per GPU-hour and lower per-token cost at scale due to amortization. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll send sample quotes.
[16:30] Priya Desai: Any compliance attestations you support? We need SOC2, ISO, and maybe regional data residencies.
[16:40] Jordan Li: We have SOC2 and ISO artifacts, and for Private we can guarantee data residency inside customer VPC/region. We'll include the compliance pack in the follow-up.
[16:55] [Short cross-talk: "thanks" "got it"]
[17:05] Samira Khan: One more practical demo — here's a quick look at how you configure a prefix cache in the Redwood Console: you create a cache rule tied to a route, specify match keys (system prompt, template id), define TTL, and enable invalidation hooks. I'll send screenshots.
[17:35] Priya Desai: Screenshots would be helpful. Also sample API calls for invalidation.
[17:42] Samira Khan: Yep, we'll share curl examples and SDK snippets.
[17:50] Noah Kim: For our use-case, I'd like to test three configurations: no-cache baseline, prefix-cache-only, prefix+KV hybrid. Can Redwood run those in a single benchmark?
[17:58] Samira Khan: Yes, we can run A/B bench where we toggle cache configs or run sequential runs and compare metrics. We'll need your traffic replay or synthetic harness.
[18:15] Priya Desai: Security note — need to confirm that cache keys do not include raw PII. We can transform keys to hashed ids upstream.
[18:25] Liam O'Connor: Good point. We typically hash user ids and strip PII before sending.
[18:32] Samira Khan: That's recommended — cache keys should be deterministic but not contain raw PII. We'll add that to the docs.
[18:45] [Audio artifact: slight echo for 2s]
[19:00] Alex Park: We're about halfway — any burning questions before we move to schedule and next steps?
[19:10] Priya Desai: One more — how do you surface cost-savings in Redwood Console? We want visibility for finance.
[19:18] Jordan Li: Console has route-level cost breakdown, token-level histograms, and an Optimize module where you can simulate cache hit rates and run sensitivity analyses. We'll give you a demo account for the pilot.
[19:35] Noah Kim: Excellent. That'll help get buy-in.
[19:40] [Slide end]
[19:50] Alex Park: Ok recap: Samira send cost model + config examples + screenshots + curl snippets; Jordan send SOC2/ISO and network diagram; Priya provide traffic profile; then we plan a benchmark for week of Sep 20.
[20:10] Priya Desai: Sounds good. We'll aim to have the profile ready by Sep 13. Security will review SOC2 docs asap.
[20:22] Alex Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
[20:28] [End of recorded transcript — rest was side chatter and calendar scheduling]
notes: Customer is payments-focused; PV: pilot in Q4; main asks: cost-model, security docs, benchmark. Agreed to hybrid deployment approach (hosted + Dedicated/VPC for regulated flows).
